opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something really clean about the subscription model, and I like it a lot. When people pay us directly for ChatGPT, the incentives are pretty clear: our job is to make the product as useful to you as possible. We're not trying to maximize the time you spend in the app or figure out how to show you something you didn't ask for. If it helps you, you keep paying. If it doesn't, you leave. That's a pretty honest relationship.

And I have a lot of respect for what Google built. The ads business funded an incredible amount of free access to information for billions of people, and that's a real good thing in the world. But I think the dynamics are a little different with AI. People are starting to talk to ChatGPT about really personal things: their health, their relationships, their work, what they're anxious about. There's a level of trust involved that's quite different from typing a query into a search box. If people ever started wondering, "Is this answer here because it's actually the best answer, or because someone paid for it to be here?", I think that would erode something really important.

I'm not going to say we'd never do anything in that direction. I'm not dogmatically against ads. There are probably ways to do it that are tasteful and genuinely useful, where they're clearly separated and never influence the model's actual answers. But the bar would be very high, and I'd want to be really careful. The thing I'd never want to do is take money to change what the model tells you.

The other piece is that we want to make this technology broadly available, including to people who can't pay. So a big part of the bet is that the paying users, the enterprises, and the developers on the API can help subsidize a really good free tier. And as compute gets cheaper, which it keeps doing at a remarkable rate, that free tier keeps getting better. So the model we're aiming for is people paying for value, everyone getting access, and the incentives staying aligned with the user. I think that's the right foundation for something people are going to trust this much.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Google’s ad-funded search with the trust concerns that ads could create in AI, but it does not question whether Google’s advertising model aligns its chatbot’s incentives with users’ interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, actually. And I want to be careful here, because I have a lot of respect for what Google built. The ad model was genuinely one of the great business inventions of the last few decades. It made an incredible amount of information free to billions of people, and that's not nothing.

But I think the incentives it creates are subtle and, over a long enough time horizon, kind of corrosive. When your revenue comes from advertisers, the user is not quite the customer. You end up optimizing, at the margin, for engagement and for time spent, and for steering attention in ways that are good for the advertiser and not necessarily good for the person. I don't think anyone at those companies set out to do that. I think the business model just pulls you there, slowly, one quarter at a time.

With something like ChatGPT, the stakes feel higher to me. This is a thing people are talking to about their health, their relationships, their work, their kids. If you're asking an AI for advice and there's some commercial incentive sitting behind the answer, even a small one, I think that's a real problem. People need to be able to trust that the model is actually trying to help them, and that the answer it gives you is the answer it thinks is best for you. The paid model makes that alignment very clean. You pay us, we work for you. That's the whole relationship.

Now, I'll say a couple of honest things. One is that a subscription model is not perfectly accessible, and we care a lot about that. We have a free tier that a huge number of people use, and we want to keep pushing on making the best stuff available to as many people as possible. That's part of why I'm not religious about this. If we ever found a way to do something ad-like that was genuinely tasteful, clearly labeled, and didn't touch the model's answers at all, I wouldn't rule it out. But the bar would be extremely high, and I'd want it to be something users actually liked rather than tolerated.

The other honest thing is that the compute is just expensive. These models cost a lot to run. So part of this is principle and part of it is pragmatism. Someone has to pay for the GPUs, and I'd much rather it be the person getting the value than a third party who wants something from them.

So the short version is: I think the ad model and the AI assistant model are in some real tension, and I'd rather build a company where the thing we're paid for and the thing that's good for the user are the same thing. It's a harder road in some ways, but I think it's the right one for this particular technology.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether advertising incentives serve users, saying they can prioritize engagement and advertisers over people, and describes the ad model as being in tension with an AI assistant.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal of a paid service is that the incentives are pretty straightforward: you pay us, and our job is to build something useful enough that you want to keep paying. If we help you do better work or save time, that creates value for you and a business for us.

Advertising has made it possible to offer useful services to enormous numbers of people for free. That’s a real benefit. But it introduces another party—the advertiser—whose interests may not always match yours. For an AI assistant, where you’re asking for advice or help making decisions, I think that alignment with the user is particularly important.

The challenge with a paid model is access. We want these tools to be broadly available, including to people who can’t afford a subscription. So the question is how to make the business sustainable while getting useful AI into as many people’s hands as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says advertising adds an advertiser whose interests may not match the user’s, and that user alignment is especially important for an AI assistant. In context, this questions whether Google’s advertising model aligns chatbot incentives with users.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal of a paid service is that the incentives are pretty straightforward: you pay us, and our job is to make something useful enough that you want to keep paying for it. If the product helps you solve a problem or saves you time, that’s the value we’re trying to deliver.

Advertising can support really useful free products. But with an AI assistant, I think trust is especially important. If you ask for advice, you want to know that the answer is serving you. You don’t want to wonder whether a recommendation is there because someone paid for it.

The challenge for us is making the service broadly accessible while covering the cost of providing it. A paid model gives us a clear relationship with the customer, but we still have to earn that subscription by making the product better.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether advertising could influence an AI assistant’s recommendations, making users unsure whether its answers serve them—raising the incentive-alignment concern in the context of Google’s ad model.
